title: Senior's toolkit: scripts that survive review
summary: The lines a reviewer expects at the top of every production script and function, and what each one prevents.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: scripts that survive review
steps.body: A scheduled script runs unattended with real permissions. These are the building blocks reviewers look for first, because each one prevents a known kind of incident.

toolkit.what: Turns silent mistakes into errors: unset variables, misspelt properties, calling functions like methods.
flags: the strictest rules of this PowerShell
only to work around legacy code, in a small scope

toolkit.what: Makes every error terminating, so the first failure stops the script or reaches your catch.
flags: on ONE call that is expected to fail
PowerShell 7.4+: a native program's non-zero exit is an error too

toolkit.what: Common parameters plus -WhatIf and -Confirm for anything that changes state.
Required inputs that can also come down the pipe; validation attributes reject bad values first.
flags: bind CSV columns or object properties by name

toolkit.what: Handle the errors you expect, specifically; always clean up.
Everything about the last error: the exception chain, the target, the script stack.
flags: PowerShell 7: the same, nicely laid out

toolkit.what: Readable long calls, and parameters built up conditionally.
The right stream for each message, so output stays clean.

pairs: A misspelt property made a report empty for months
A clean-up deleted the wrong folder with no dry run
A failed run left its lock file forever

steps.prompt: In PowerShell 7.4+, a script runs `git push` and git fails with exit code 1. What makes the script stop there, like a failing cmdlet would?
options: Nothing can: always check `$LASTEXITCODE` by hand
steps.explain: By default a native program's exit code only sets `$LASTEXITCODE` (and `$?`). Since 7.4 the preference variable turns a non-zero exit into a PowerShell error, which `'Stop'` makes terminating. In Windows PowerShell 5.1 you check `$LASTEXITCODE` yourself (module 6).

steps.prompt: The first lines of a production script.
steps.explain: `#Requires` first, then `[CmdletBinding()]` and `param()` (which must be the first statement), then strict mode and the error preference.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Start every script from the same template: `#Requires`, comment-based help, `[CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)]`, `param()`, `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest`, `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'`. Catch per item in loops, report, and exit non-zero when anything failed.
